payload.title: Decouple Endless sessions from harness session identity with a session_instances table
payload.description: Claude Code mints a NEW session UUID on a clear while the Endless session, the tmux window and the task are all unchanged (verified: CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID 738849b7 -> 8735f6a4, same CLAUDE_PID 18201). sessions.session_id stores that UUID, so the intended invariant — one Endless session per task, forever — breaks the moment a user clears. Move harness identity off sessions into a child table: one durable Endless session (sessions.id, which Endless mints and owns) with an ordered sequence of harness instances beneath it; a clear appends an instance instead of minting a second sessions row. Upstream of E-1983, now unblocked and otherwise built against the old model, and of the write-once task_id tightening. Design, verified codebase facts and the one open decision are in --analysis.

triage.rationale: the description defers the schema shape and the "one open decision" to the --analysis attachment rather than pinning them down here, so an implementer can't proceed from this text alone.

fields.analysis:
# Why harness identity cannot live on `sessions`

`sessions.session_id` holds the harness's own conversation id. The harness
replaces that id at its own discretion, so it is not an identity Endless can
build an invariant on.

Measured, not assumed (2026-08-16):

- A clear mints a new `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` — observed `738849b7…` becoming
  `8735f6a4…` — while `CLAUDE_PID` stayed `18201`. Same process, same tmux
  window, same task, new conversation id.
- `claude --resume <uuid>` does NOT mint. Session 1067 kept UUID `70e685df…`
  from 2026-08-12 to 2026-08-16.
- Compaction does NOT mint either. Session 1067 spanned a very long conversation
  that was certainly compacted and never changed id. This matters because
  compaction is automatic and unavoidable; had it rotated the id, any invariant
  keyed on the id would have been unworkable rather than merely leaky.

So: resume preserves, compaction preserves, a clear rotates.

## The anchor has to be an id Endless mints and owns

That is `sessions.id`. Everything the harness issues is a handle it may replace.

Two anchors were considered and rejected, both worth recording so they are not
revisited:

- **`CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`** — rotates on clear, which is the whole problem.
- **`CLAUDE_PID`** — rejected for three independent reasons, any one fatal. A
  resumed-but-not-running session has no PID at all at resolution time; a closed
  and later resumed session gets a different PID, so the invariant would not
  survive the gap it most needs to; and the OS recycles PIDs, which converts a
  correctness bug into an intermittent one. The general error was reaching for a
  RUNTIME HANDLE as a DURABLE IDENTITY.

## Shape

One `sessions` row per task (durable), with an ordered sequence of harness
instances beneath it. A clear appends an instance. Transcript rows FK to the
instance, not to the session, so a clear simply gives subsequent rows a new
parent and no prior row is rewritten.

Per-harness identity goes in per-harness tables joined by a composite FK against
`UNIQUE (id, harness)` on the base, so a `claude_cli_sessions` row physically
cannot attach to an instance belonging to a different harness. The single-table
alternative (harness identity columns on the base) was REJECTED by the
requester: it bakes one harness's identity model — single value, UUID-shaped,
rotating — into the shared table, and none of that is known to hold for the
next harness. `internal/hookcmd/codex.go` already exists, so the second harness
is not hypothetical.

**`platform` moves off `sessions` onto the instance.** Decided. `sessions` today
carries `platform TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'claude'`; leaving it there would both
duplicate the instance's harness discriminator and make sequential cross-harness
work impossible by construction. The rule settled on: the same task may NOT be
worked by two harnesses concurrently (that is the one-live-instance violation
regardless of harness), but MAY be worked by different harnesses in sequence —
which falls out for free once the Endless session is harness-neutral.

## Ordering and selection

Order instances by `first_seen_at` ASCENDING, never by recency, and show recency
as a column. `first_seen_at` never moves, so instance 1 is always the
pre-clear conversation.

The failure case that forces this: a task runs for a week, is cleared midway,
and the real work lands in instance 2. The user later resumes instance 1 just to
read something, which bumps its recency and makes the half-finished conversation
look like the one to resume. **Recency and relevance diverge exactly when the
stakes are highest.** "Which instance should be resumed" is therefore not
derivable and must not be guessed.

## OPEN DECISION — do not resolve alone

How to enforce one-open-instance. At most two of:

- **(a)** DB-enforced, via `UNIQUE (session_id) WHERE ended_at IS NULL`
- **(b)** no auto-close
- **(c)** no permanent block after a crash

The requester wants (a) and (b) emphatically, which forces (c). Mechanism: the
index makes uniqueness on `session_id` among rows where `ended_at IS NULL`, so a
crashed instance whose `ended_at` was never set keeps that session's one open
slot forever, and the next resume fails the constraint. Hooks cannot self-heal
it: the "clear `ended_at` when an instance emits an event" rule only ever fires
for the LIVE instance, never for the dead one. The codebase already concedes the
premise — `internal/hookcmd/claude.go:147`, on the SessionEnd lock release: "if
it fails to fire (missing, crashed, misconfigured), the lock leaks."

Auto-close on SessionStart would fix it, and the requester has explicitly ruled
it out: prior auto-close behaviour caused real damage and is not to be repeated
without certainty that no live session can be closed.

**Unanswered proposal, offered as the fourth way out:** keep `ended_at` for
DISPLAY ONLY, drop the partial unique index entirely, and have `resume` refuse
when it finds 2+ open instances — list them and let the user close one.
Enforcement lands where a human is present to judge, nothing is ever closed
automatically, and a stale `ended_at` renders as "unknown" rather than blocking.
It reuses the resume-disambiguation listing the design already needs. The cost
is that the guarantee moves from the storage layer to the CLI, which is the
weaker layer.

## Consequences for neighbouring commands

- **`spawn --reopen` collapses into `reopen` + `resume`.** `--reopen` currently
  does three separable things — flip a terminal task status back to workable,
  restore the worktree (reuse, or rebuild off main if reaped), and attach a
  session — plus a fourth path that navigates to a live owner instead of
  spawning. That last path is already `resume`'s behaviour. Split by what
  changes: `reopen` is a task-status verb, `resume` is a session verb that
  restores the worktree and navigates when the session is live.
- **`--new-session` should be deleted, not reinterpreted.** It exists to refuse
  inheriting the prior session's context. Under one-session-per-task it is
  incoherent: "start a new session" would have to mint a second `sessions` row
  for the task. Its only legitimate residue is "do not inject prior context into
  the handoff", which is a handoff-content flag (`--fresh-context`), not a
  session-identity one. The original motivation is unknown; the code comment
  cites E-894, but that task is "Move task display reads from Python to Go" and
  is a pointer to the mechanism, not the origin.

## Facts a planning session should not re-derive

- **Liveness is DERIVED, not stored** (E-1898, `internal/monitor/liveness.go`,
  states include `unbound`). It removed `sessions.process` precisely to stop
  storing liveness. `ended_at` therefore needs a deliberate justification rather
  than being added by reflex — the requester's position is that it is
  informational (which instance to resume), not operational.
- **Liveness cannot be derived inside SQLite.** It requires inspecting processes
  and tmux. A partial index can only reference stored columns, and a trigger
  cannot shell out. So DB-level enforcement REQUIRES some stored open/closed
  state; there is no purely-derived version of option (a).
- **`payload.Source`** (`startup` / `resume` / `clear` / `compact`) is declared
  on `claudePayload` and read NOWHERE. It is the field that distinguishes "the
  same work continuing" from "a different session took this window".
- **Hooks pin to main.** `endless-go hook` calls `PinMainDB`, and a
  cwd-self-detected sandbox deliberately does NOT suppress that pin (E-1700), so
  hook writes always reach the real ledger. Only an explicit `--config-dir`
  overrides it, and only tests pass that. Consequence worth knowing before
  adding any auto-close: a test that drives real hooks is one missing
  `--config-dir` away from mutating real sessions — `tests/tasks/e-1953-verify.sh`
  depends on exactly that flag today.
- Endless deals in tmux WINDOWS, not tmux sessions.

## About the exploratory report

`docs/private/research-2026-08-16-harness-sessions.md` records the wider option
space and is worth reading, with one correction: its "Facts" section states
"`sessions` has exactly one row per task. Period." and "a task is spawned
exactly once". Those are the requester's INTENDED INVARIANTS, not descriptions
of the database. Today, real (non-fixture) tasks carry up to 7 `sessions` rows —
1307 has 7, 1362 and 1322 have 6 — created by `spawn --reopen --new-session`.
Collapsing those into one session row plus N instance rows is migration work
this task owns. No task currently has 2+ NON-ended sessions, so the invariant is
not being violated live; it is simply not yet enforced.

# Largely subsumed by write-once `sessions.task_id` (E-1969 and the tightening)

Re-analysed 2026-08-16 after the requester pointed out that a bind which can
never be reassigned is the FEATURE, not the failure. They are right, and the
original framing of this task was wrong.

## Why write-once fixes the reported symptom

`session resume E-1953` resumes an EXISTING Claude session by UUID, so the
`sessions` row already exists with `task_id = 1953`. `trySpawnBind` firing at
SessionStart is therefore a REASSIGNMENT of an already-bound session, not a
first bind. Under write-once semantics that write is refused and E-1953 stands.
No marker change needed for this case.

That is the entirety of the reported incident (twice), so the tightening
resolves it.

## The residual case, which write-once makes WORSE rather than better

A genuinely NEW Claude session started in a window left over from a previous
spawn. There the stale marker is the FIRST write, so write-once cements the
wrong task permanently — and the manual `task bind` recovery is gone by design.

Scope of that risk, measured rather than assumed:

- `task spawn` always creates a FRESH tmux window (`new-window`) and sets
  `@endless_spawned_by`, `@endless_task_id`, `@endless_project_id` on it
  (spawnlaunchcmd/tmux_driver.go, windowOptionCommands).
- Nothing anywhere clears any of the three.
- So the markers are per-window and die with the window. Exposure is confined
  to a spawned window that OUTLIVES its session and is then reused for
  something else.

That is narrow, but it is not theoretical: it is exactly the shape of the
incident that produced this task, differing only in whether the session was
resumed or fresh.

## Recommended shape, if it is still worth doing

CORRECTION (2026-08-16): an earlier draft of this analysis said not to clear the
window variables because it would break the E-1700 read race. That was wrong.
E-1700's race is `@endless_task_id` reading EMPTY, in which case `trySpawnBind`
returns false and binds nothing — so the variables must survive that path for
the retry, and they do. Clearing only after a bind SUCCEEDS preserves the retry
entirely.

So the fix is the obvious one: **`trySpawnBind` clears `@endless_spawned_by`
and `@endless_task_id` once it has successfully bound.** One spawn, one bind.
A later session starting in the same window finds nothing and falls through to
the cwd-based bind, which is correct for it.

Recording an expected session identity at spawn time is NOT viable as an
alternative: `task spawn` launches `claude` and the Claude session UUID does not
exist until the process starts, so spawn has nothing to record.

## Sequencing

Blocked on the write-once change rather than duplicating it. If that lands
first, re-scope this to the residual case only; the title should change with it,
since "clear the markers" is no longer the recommended fix.

## Requester position (2026-08-16): enforce the invariant, don't tolerate the breach

`tmux window == Claude session == Endless task` is to be treated as an
invariant. A new Claude session starting in a window left over from a previous
spawn should be made to FAIL, not quietly bound to something. Allowing the
invariant to break cascades: the tmux status line already resolves by WINDOW,
not pane, so a window associated with two sessions is ambiguous to it
independently of any binding bug.

Two mechanical facts that constrain how this can be built:

1. **SessionStart cannot hard-refuse a session.** The hook's only lever there is
   `additionalContext` — `handleWorktreeAdoption` already returns a "refusal"
   that is nothing more than injected text. Making a session genuinely unusable
   requires blocking at PreToolUse, which is the shape `enforceWorktreeGate` and
   `enforceClaimedCwd` already use. So "fail to run" = inform at SessionStart +
   block tool calls at PreToolUse.

2. **E-1669 faced this choice and went the other way**, deliberately: "A
   warning, NOT a refuse: refusing in the hook path blocks every tool call."
   That was the right call for its risk (a session dogfooding the wrong binary).
   The risk here is different in kind — under write-once `task_id` a mis-bind is
   permanent and has no recovery — which is what justifies the stronger
   response rather than copying E-1669's.

**Ship an escape hatch with the gate, or the gate becomes the bug.** Nothing in
the codebase clears `@endless_spawned_by` / `@endless_task_id` /
`@endless_project_id` today. If a window can be refused on the strength of those
markers, there must be a supported way to reset them — otherwise the first false
positive strands a tmux window permanently and the only workaround a user will
find is killing the window or disabling the gate.

Relationship to the identity-scoping fix above: they do different jobs and both
are worth having. Identity-scoped markers stop the WRONG BIND (a fresh session
falls through to the cwd bind, which is correct). The refusal enforces the
INVARIANT, which matters beyond binding because window-keyed resolution exists
elsewhere. Scoping is the narrower, safer change; refusal is the architectural
one and carries the false-positive risk.

# Addendum — E-1969 landed; re-scoped to the residual case (2026-08-25)

Written from ES's E-1969 session at Mike's request. Evidence and scope only; the
choice between the two shapes below is still Mike's to
settle.

## The reported symptom is now fixed, in the database

`sessions.task_id` is write-once as of E-1969, enforced by the
`sessions_task_id_write_once` trigger. The resume case plays out like this now,
verified against the shipped code:

1. `trySpawnBind` reads the stale `@endless_task_id` and calls
   `BindSessionToTask`.
2. The row already holds a task, so the write is a reassignment and the trigger
   aborts it. `BindSessionToTask` returns an error naming "write-once".
3. `trySpawnBind` logs and returns FALSE, so `maybeCwdBind` runs
   `autoBindFromCwd`, which E-1856 already guards against re-pointing.
4. The correct binding stands.

No marker change is needed for that case. `session resume E-1953` can no longer
be stolen by a leftover marker.

## What is left, and why write-once makes it worse

A genuinely NEW session in a window a previous spawn left behind. `task_id` is
NULL, so the stale marker is the FIRST write and the trigger PERMITS it. The
wrong task is then permanent: E-1968 made `task bind` first-set-only and E-1969
enforces it in the database, so the manual recovery this task's original
incident used is gone by design.

Before E-1969 this was a recoverable annoyance. After it, it is unrecoverable.
That inversion is the whole remaining case, and it is the reason to keep this
task open rather than close it as subsumed.

## Defect in the recommended shape above — do not build it as written

The "Recommended shape" section says `trySpawnBind` should clear
`@endless_spawned_by` AND `@endless_task_id` once it has bound. Clearing
`@endless_spawned_by` is wrong: it is not only a bind trigger.
`monitor.ResolveSessionStatusParentSession` reads that same window option to
render the `from` provenance row in `session status`
(`internal/monitor/session_status.go`, and the note at
`internal/sessionstatuscmd/session_status.go` about keeping that row testable
headless). Clearing it at the first SessionStart erases the window's parent-
session link for the rest of its life.

CORRECTION, same day: the two paragraphs that stood here proposed unsetting
`@endless_task_id` instead, and a new `@endless_bound_session` option as a
variant. Both were wrong. See "Unsetting any marker is out" and "The window
already carries the facts" below, which replace them. Recorded rather than
deleted because the reasoning that produced them is the thing to avoid
repeating.

E-1700's retry is unaffected by any of this and is worth keeping straight: that
race is `@endless_task_id` reading EMPTY, in which case `trySpawnBind` returns
false and binds nothing, so the next SessionStart retries.

## Unsetting any marker is out

Not "clear `@endless_spawned_by` but `@endless_task_id` is fine" — unsetting is
wrong for either one, for two independent reasons.

**It destroys a value other readers depend on.** `@endless_task_id` is not only
`trySpawnBind`'s trigger. `session status`'s focal-task resolution falls back to
it ("live session's active task, else the window's `@endless_task_id`", per the
`session_status` docstring in the Python CLI), and E-1302 proposes exposing it
as `endless tmux task`. Unsetting makes the window anonymous to all of them.

**It conflates two states that must stay distinct.** Unset would mean "this
spawn was already used", and unset ALSO means "this window was never a spawn
window". After unsetting, nothing can tell them apart. Encoding a fact by
destroying the evidence for it is the class of write E-1898 removed from
`sessions`, and for the same reason: the erased value is exactly what you need
when the thing goes wrong.

## The window already carries the facts — the question is which id is durable

A spawned window carries four options today:

    @endless_project_id    @endless_spawned_by
    @endless_task_id       @endless_session_uuid

`@endless_session_uuid` is E-1585's, written by `setTmuxSessionUUID` in
`internal/hookcmd/claude.go`, so no new option needs inventing to record "which
session is in this window".

Two facts about it that constrain how it can be used, and one conclusion.

**Today it is overwritten on EVERY event**, before the SessionStart handling
that would read it — deliberately, so it self-heals after a tmux server restart.
As written it therefore records the most recent session in the window, not the
one the window was spawned for.

**Freezing it would be the wrong fix.** The value is a harness-issued
conversation id, and E-2063 measured that a clear rotates it (resume and
compaction do not). Making a rotating handle sticky does not turn it into an
identity; it turns it into a stale handle, and it breaks what E-1585 built the
option FOR — a sibling shell pane reading it to discover the Claude session
beside it would resolve a conversation that no longer exists. E-2063 names this
error class directly, in rejecting `CLAUDE_PID` as an anchor: "the general error
was reaching for a RUNTIME HANDLE as a DURABLE IDENTITY."

**So publish the id Endless owns instead.** Once E-2063 exists that is
`sessions.id`, which never rotates — at which point overwrite-vs-write-once
stops being a question at all, because writing the same value every event is
idempotent. The option stays self-healing AND stable across a clear, with no
invariant to enforce. This is the same move E-1969 made one table over:
`sessions.task_id` is write-once because Endless mints it; `sessions.session_id`
is not that kind of id, which is why E-2063 moves it out rather than freezing
it.

## E-1128 wants the opposite of a clear

E-1128 ("Record spawn lineage on `endless task spawn`", unplanned) treats
`@endless_spawned_by` as durable lineage. Partly stale — the marker exists today
and is already read for the provenance row — but whichever branch is chosen here
must not erase it, or E-1128's premise goes with it.

## Why Branch B is not merely a bigger Branch A

`monitor.GetTaskForPane` resolves pane-specific first, then falls back to WINDOW
scope: any pane in the same window with a non-NULL `task_id`, most recent
`last_activity` winning. So a window that has hosted two sessions on two tasks
gives the status line an answer decided by a timestamp race, independently of
whether either binding was correct. Marker scoping does not touch that; the
invariant gate is what would. Branch A fixes an instance, Branch B fixes a
class. That is the real difference between them, and it is not visible from the
binding bug alone.

## Sequencing note

E-1972 (underway) may invert which binary runs the Claude hooks. Whatever lands
here lives in `internal/hookcmd/claude.go` on the SessionStart path, so it will
sit underneath that decision. Not a conflict — overlap to coordinate, in that
order.

---

# The invariant, as the requester states it (2026-08-25)

Superseding the 2026-08-16 "Requester position" section above, which said
`tmux window == Claude session == Endless task`. That form cannot hold, because
a clear mints a new harness session id. The form that does:

    tmux window == Endless task == one or more Claude sessions

with two explicit non-accommodations:

- NOT multiple CONCURRENT sessions for the same task.
- NOT multiple ACTIVE tmux windows for the same task.

Sessions in SERIES are accommodated; sessions in PARALLEL are not. That is the
whole of it, and it is what makes the gate expressible: the thing being counted
is the Endless session, not the harness conversation.

# What this leaves to decide

E-2063 blocks this task and changes what the gate can be built on. With a
durable `sessions.id` on the window, the question stops being "which of two
shapes" and becomes a single one:

**What does the gate compare, and what does it do on a mismatch?**

The comparison has a real candidate that needs no marker mutation: the window's
task id versus the task the cwd resolves to (`resolveCwdTaskID`, the signal
`autoBindFromCwd` already trusts). Agreement is the ordinary case; disagreement
on a genuinely new session is the invariant breach.

`payload.Source` (`startup` / `resume` / `clear` / `compact`) is declared on
`claudePayload` and read nowhere — E-2063 records this too, and calls it "the
field that distinguishes 'the same work continuing' from 'a different session
took this window'". Under E-2063 it may not be needed for this gate at all,
since a clear stops minting a second Endless session; note it and do not build
on it before that lands.

Still open regardless of shape: the escape hatch. Nothing clears any of the four
window options today, so a window refused on their strength has no supported
reset, and the first false positive strands it. That requirement survives every
version of this task.

# Corrections to the addendum above, for the record

- The addendum's "Defect in the recommended shape" originally concluded that
  `@endless_task_id` could be consumed by unsetting. Replaced in place; see
  "Unsetting any marker is out".
- An earlier draft of this analysis cited E-1640 as evidence that a succession
  of session rows per window is normal and supported. That inverts what E-1640
  says: it is titled "Fix duplicate session rows minted per Claude launch when
  TMUX_PANE is empty" and its remedy ENDS the extra rows. It treated the
  succession as a defect to suppress, which is the opposite of blessing it.
  E-2063 is where that model actually changes.

fields.description: Post-E-1969 residual of the original marker bug. `task spawn` sets @endless_task_id on a new tmux window and nothing clears it, so `trySpawnBind` binds every later SessionStart in that window to the spawned task. Write-once fixed the RESUMED case — that write is now a refused reassignment — but made the FRESH-session case unrecoverable: on a session whose task_id is NULL the stale marker is the FIRST write, the trigger permits it, and `task bind` can no longer move it. Now blocked on E-2063, which gives the window a durable Endless session id to compare against. Settled since 2026-08-16: unsetting markers is out, no new window option is needed, and the invariant is `tmux window == Endless task == one or more Claude sessions` — in series, never concurrent. What remains to decide is what the gate compares and what it does on a mismatch, plus the escape hatch every version of this needs. See --analysis.

# Why harness identity cannot live on `sessions`

`sessions.session_id` holds the harness's own conversation id. The harness
replaces that id at its own discretion, so it is not an identity Endless can
build an invariant on.

Measured, not assumed (2026-08-16):

- A clear mints a new `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` — observed `738849b7…` becoming
  `8735f6a4…` — while `CLAUDE_PID` stayed `18201`. Same process, same tmux
  window, same task, new conversation id.
- `claude --resume <uuid>` does NOT mint. Session 1067 kept UUID `70e685df…`
  from 2026-08-12 to 2026-08-16.
- Compaction does NOT mint either. Session 1067 spanned a very long conversation
  that was certainly compacted and never changed id. This matters because
  compaction is automatic and unavoidable; had it rotated the id, any invariant
  keyed on the id would have been unworkable rather than merely leaky.

So: resume preserves, compaction preserves, a clear rotates.

## The anchor has to be an id Endless mints and owns

That is `sessions.id`. Everything the harness issues is a handle it may replace.

Two anchors were considered and rejected, both worth recording so they are not
revisited:

- **`CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`** — rotates on clear, which is the whole problem.
- **`CLAUDE_PID`** — rejected for three independent reasons, any one fatal. A
  resumed-but-not-running session has no PID at all at resolution time; a closed
  and later resumed session gets a different PID, so the invariant would not
  survive the gap it most needs to; and the OS recycles PIDs, which converts a
  correctness bug into an intermittent one. The general error was reaching for a
  RUNTIME HANDLE as a DURABLE IDENTITY.

## Shape

One `sessions` row per task (durable), with an ordered sequence of harness
instances beneath it. A clear appends an instance. Transcript rows FK to the
instance, not to the session, so a clear simply gives subsequent rows a new
parent and no prior row is rewritten.

Per-harness identity goes in per-harness tables joined by a composite FK against
`UNIQUE (id, harness)` on the base, so a `claude_cli_sessions` row physically
cannot attach to an instance belonging to a different harness. The single-table
alternative (harness identity columns on the base) was REJECTED by the
requester: it bakes one harness's identity model — single value, UUID-shaped,
rotating — into the shared table, and none of that is known to hold for the
next harness. `internal/hookcmd/codex.go` already exists, so the second harness
is not hypothetical.

**`platform` moves off `sessions` onto the instance.** Decided. `sessions` today
carries `platform TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'claude'`; leaving it there would both
duplicate the instance's harness discriminator and make sequential cross-harness
work impossible by construction. The rule settled on: the same task may NOT be
worked by two harnesses concurrently (that is the one-live-instance violation
regardless of harness), but MAY be worked by different harnesses in sequence —
which falls out for free once the Endless session is harness-neutral.

## Ordering and selection

Order instances by `first_seen_at` ASCENDING, never by recency, and show recency
as a column. `first_seen_at` never moves, so instance 1 is always the
pre-clear conversation.

The failure case that forces this: a task runs for a week, is cleared midway,
and the real work lands in instance 2. The user later resumes instance 1 just to
read something, which bumps its recency and makes the half-finished conversation
look like the one to resume. **Recency and relevance diverge exactly when the
stakes are highest.** "Which instance should be resumed" is therefore not
derivable and must not be guessed.

## DECIDED (2026-08-25): no DB constraint; enforce at resume

`ended_at` is DISPLAY ONLY. No `UNIQUE (session_id) WHERE ended_at IS NULL`
index. `resume` refuses when it finds 2+ open instances for a session, lists
them, and lets the user close one. Nothing is ever closed automatically. A stale
`ended_at` renders as "unknown" rather than blocking anything.

This resolves a collision between two positions the requester had both stated:
`ended_at` is informational, AND the uniqueness constraint was wanted. The index
makes `ended_at` a constraint predicate, which is operational by definition, so
the two could not both hold.

The reasoning that settled it, in the requester's words: storage is the more
reliable layer only in the absolute — "when unreliable things are in charge of
writing to storage then the storage itself becomes unreliable." `ended_at` is
written by hooks; hooks fail open by design and do not fire on a crash. An index
over hook-written data does not contain that unreliability, it AMPLIFIES it,
converting "this row is stale" into "this write is refused". The failure mode of
the constraint is strictly worse than the failure mode it was meant to catch.

Consequences that follow and should not be re-litigated:

- The crash case stops mattering. A crashed instance leaves a stale open row;
  nothing reads it operationally, so nothing wedges. `resume` shows it as
  "unknown" alongside the recap and the user picks.
- Auto-close is not needed anywhere, which was the requirement — prior
  auto-close behaviour caused real damage.
- Enforcement of one-live-instance moves entirely to the hook-level invariant
  gate (E-1983) plus write-once `task_id`. Those are now the only things
  preventing genuine concurrency, so they carry more weight than they did when a
  DB constraint was assumed to be the backstop.
- Reuses the resume-disambiguation listing this design already needs; no new
  surface.

## Consequences for neighbouring commands

- **`spawn --reopen` collapses into `reopen` + `resume`.** `--reopen` currently
  does three separable things — flip a terminal task status back to workable,
  restore the worktree (reuse, or rebuild off main if reaped), and attach a
  session — plus a fourth path that navigates to a live owner instead of
  spawning. That last path is already `resume`'s behaviour. Split by what
  changes: `reopen` is a task-status verb, `resume` is a session verb that
  restores the worktree and navigates when the session is live.
- **`--new-session` should be deleted, not reinterpreted.** It exists to refuse
  inheriting the prior session's context. Under one-session-per-task it is
  incoherent: "start a new session" would have to mint a second `sessions` row
  for the task. Its only legitimate residue is "do not inject prior context into
  the handoff", which is a handoff-content flag (`--fresh-context`), not a
  session-identity one. The original motivation is unknown; the code comment
  cites E-894, but that task is "Move task display reads from Python to Go" and
  is a pointer to the mechanism, not the origin.

## Facts a planning session should not re-derive

- **Liveness is DERIVED, not stored** (E-1898, `internal/monitor/liveness.go`,
  states include `unbound`). It removed `sessions.process` precisely to stop
  storing liveness. `ended_at` therefore needs a deliberate justification rather
  than being added by reflex — the requester's position is that it is
  informational (which instance to resume), not operational.
- **Liveness cannot be derived inside SQLite.** It requires inspecting processes
  and tmux. A partial index can only reference stored columns, and a trigger
  cannot shell out. So DB-level enforcement REQUIRES some stored open/closed
  state; there is no purely-derived version of option (a).
- **`payload.Source`** (`startup` / `resume` / `clear` / `compact`) is declared
  on `claudePayload` and read NOWHERE. It is the field that distinguishes "the
  same work continuing" from "a different session took this window".
- **Hooks pin to main.** `endless-go hook` calls `PinMainDB`, and a
  cwd-self-detected sandbox deliberately does NOT suppress that pin (E-1700), so
  hook writes always reach the real ledger. Only an explicit `--config-dir`
  overrides it, and only tests pass that. Consequence worth knowing before
  adding any auto-close: a test that drives real hooks is one missing
  `--config-dir` away from mutating real sessions — `tests/tasks/e-1953-verify.sh`
  depends on exactly that flag today.
- Endless deals in tmux WINDOWS, not tmux sessions.

## About the exploratory report

`docs/private/research-2026-08-16-harness-sessions.md` records the wider option
space and is worth reading, with one correction: its "Facts" section states
"`sessions` has exactly one row per task. Period." and "a task is spawned
exactly once". Those are the requester's INTENDED INVARIANTS, not descriptions
of the database. Today, real (non-fixture) tasks carry up to 7 `sessions` rows —
1307 has 7, 1362 and 1322 have 6 — created by `spawn --reopen --new-session`.
Collapsing those into one session row plus N instance rows is migration work

not being violated live; it is simply not yet enforced.

# Plan: stop `rebuild-db --confirm` deleting rows it is about to re-insert

## The open question, answered: neither clause yields

The description framed this as trigger-versus-FK — ED-1560 says the binding is
never cleared, `ON DELETE SET NULL` says it is cleared with the task, so one of
them has to give. That framing is wrong, and measuring the damage is what shows
it.

Drop the trigger on a fresh schema, run `rebuild-db`'s own two statements, and
this is what a "rebuild" does:

    before: landings=1  sessions.task_id=5  session_statuses.task_id=5
    after : landings=0  sessions.task_id=None  session_statuses.task_id=None

Every FK referencing `tasks(id)` fires, and the re-insert restores none of it:

| Referencing column              | On delete | Restored by the re-insert? |
|---------------------------------|-----------|----------------------------|
| `task_landings.task_id`         | CASCADE   | **no — the rows are gone** |
| `session_gates.epic_id`         | CASCADE   | no                         |
| `sessions.task_id`              | SET NULL  | no                         |
| `sessions.epic_id`              | SET NULL  | no                         |
| `session_statuses.task_id`      | SET NULL  | no                         |
| `decisions.origin_task_id`      | SET NULL  | yes (decisions are replaced too) |
| `tasks.parent_id`               | SET NULL  | yes (tasks are replaced)   |

So the write-once trigger is not the other side of a contradiction. It is a
**fuse**, and it has been catching a wrecking ball. Removing it — or removing
the FK action it fires on — converts a loud abort into the silent destruction of
every landing record in the database.

That settles it: **the FK stays, the trigger stays, and `rebuild-db` is what
changes.** A wholesale replacement of a table should not be spelled as a
deletion of that table.

### Why not `PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF` around the swap

It is the smaller change — no generated SQL, no column list, just fence the
existing two statements — and it does work: with enforcement off the DELETE
performs no action, so the landings survive and the tasks come back.

Rejected on one ground, and NOT on the one you might expect. `monitor.DB()` calls
`SetMaxOpenConns(1)`, so the connection-scoped PRAGMA and the transaction are
guaranteed to share a connection; the pooling hazard is not real here. What is
real: SQLite ignores `PRAGMA foreign_keys` inside a transaction, so the fence has
to sit outside `Begin()`/`Commit()` — and then a genuinely-lost task id is
deleted with enforcement off, leaving `task_landings` rows pointing at a task
that no longer exists. That trades a loud abort for silent corruption, which is
the same trade dropping the trigger would make. §1 avoids the deletion instead of
suppressing the checking, and that is the difference worth the extra code.

Confirmed end to end against the real binary and the modernc driver, not just
`sqlite3` in Python:

    Projection: 1 events replayed, 1 tasks created, 0 updated, 0 deleted
    endless-go event: error clearing tasks: constraint failed:
      sessions.task_id is write-once (1811)

## 1. Replace the tasks swap with an upsert, and prune only what vanished

In `runRebuildDB` (`internal/eventcmd/event.go`), the pair

    DELETE FROM tasks WHERE project_id IN (...)
    INSERT INTO tasks SELECT * FROM proj.tasks

becomes an upsert that never deletes a row it is about to re-insert, followed by
a prune of the ids the projection genuinely no longer has:

    INSERT INTO tasks SELECT * FROM proj.tasks
      ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET <col> = excluded.<col>, ...

    DELETE FROM tasks
     WHERE project_id IN (...)
       AND id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM proj.tasks)

**Build the `DO UPDATE SET` column list at runtime from
`pragma_table_info('tasks')`, minus `id`.** Hand-writing it would be a second
copy of the schema to keep in sync, and the existing `SELECT *` already depends
on column order matching between the two databases — deriving the list from the
live table keeps that dependency in one place instead of two. Keep the E-1929
comment about `removed`: raw `tasks` on both sides, never `live_tasks`.

An unchanged rebuild — the common case, and the only case anyone runs
deliberately — now touches no FK at all, because nothing is deleted.

## 2. The prune can still abort, and that abort is correct

A task present in the database but absent from the projection is still deleted,
and if a session is bound to it the trigger still fires. Do not weaken this.
That case means the ledger no longer knows about a task some session claimed,
and destroying the evidence of that claim is exactly what E-1967 exists to
prevent.

Make it a **named refusal before the transaction opens**, not a raw SQLite
message from inside it:

- Compute the prune set (`tasks` in scope, `id NOT IN proj.tasks`).
- If any of them is referenced by `sessions.task_id` or has a `task_landings`
  row, refuse, listing the task ids and which record would be destroyed.
- Otherwise prune normally.

The message must say what the state means — the ledger is missing history the
database has — rather than telling the user to force anything. There is no
`--force` here to add.

## 3. Surface the prune set in the dry run

`rebuild-db` without `--confirm` already prints its projection counts and stops.
It should also print what the prune would remove, and whether any of it would be
refused by §2. Today the dry run tells you nothing about the destructive half of
the command, which is the half worth previewing.

## 4. Replace `task_landings` from the projection too

`replayTaskLanded` already populates `task_landings` in the projection temp
database. `runRebuildDB` never copies it back, so a rebuild silently declines to
rebuild a table the projector went to the trouble of building. That is folded in
here rather than filed, because it is not adjacent to §1 — it is entangled with
it (ED-1550: fold a finding into an open task rather than growing the backlog).

The entanglement, stated so it is not rediscovered the hard way: the schema
comment on `task_landings_notify_sessions` (E-2005) currently reads

> A full-ledger replay fires this too … Harmless: that DB has no sessions … and
> `event rebuild` copies back only tasks, decisions and decision_relations —
> never session_notices.

That "harmless" is load-bearing on the omission this section removes. Copy
landings into the REAL database and the trigger fires there, against real
`sessions` and `session_tasks`, announcing every historical landing to every
live session as though it had just happened.

So the copy is three things, not one:

1. **Suppress the notice trigger for the duration.** `DROP TRIGGER
   task_landings_notify_sessions`, copy, re-`CREATE` it — inside the
   transaction, so a rollback restores it. SQLite takes DDL transactionally, and
   `internal/schema/changes/e-1969-rename-sessions-task-id.go` already
   establishes the drop-copy-recreate shape. Keep the trigger body in ONE place
   (ED-1472) rather than pasting a second copy into Go.

2. **Null a `session_id` the real database does not have.** The projected value
   comes from the ledger event's actor, and the ledger is shareable while
   `sessions` is machine-local — so a landing recorded on another machine names
   a session id this database has never seen. `task_landings.session_id`
   references `sessions(id)` with `ON DELETE SET NULL`, so the insert would fail
   the FK outright. NULL is the honest value and the one the FK itself would
   arrive at.

3. **Do not carry the projection's `id` values across.** Nothing references
   `task_landings.id`; let the real table assign its own.

Scope the replacement the same way tasks are scoped — landings whose `task_id`
is in `proj.tasks` — so a rebuild of one project cannot clear another's.

**Correct the E-2005 comment in the same commit.** Leaving it saying `event
rebuild` copies back only three tables would leave two comments in the tree
contradicting each other, which is the exact failure E-1967 cleaned up in
`execTaskReleased`.

## Do NOT touch decisions / decision_relations

Their only dependent (`decision_relations` on `decisions`, CASCADE) is itself
replaced from the projection in the same transaction, so that delete-and-insert
is self-consistent in a way the tasks one is not. Changing it would be churn.

## Verification

- A rebuild of an unchanged ledger, on a database with a bound session and a
  landing record, completes — and afterwards the binding, the landing row and
  the `session_statuses.task_id` are all exactly as they were.
- The same rebuild leaves the tasks table byte-identical to what the old
  delete-and-insert produced, for a projection that has every existing id.
- A task the projection has dropped, with no session binding and no landing, is
  pruned.
- A task the projection has dropped that a session is bound to is REFUSED, by
  name, before anything is written — and the database is untouched afterwards.
- The write-once trigger and every `REFERENCES tasks(id)` clause are unchanged:
  assert the schema still declares them, so a later sweep cannot "fix" this by
  removing the fuse.
- `pragma_table_info`-driven column list: adding a column to `tasks` needs no
  edit here. Assert by rebuilding after adding a scratch column.
- A rebuild restores `task_landings` from the ledger: destroy the rows first,
  rebuild, and the landing history comes back with its branch, base branch and
  merge sha intact.
- A rebuild with a live session and historical landings writes ZERO rows to
  `session_notices`. This is the one that would otherwise ship as a flood of
  "your task landed" notices for work that landed weeks ago.
- The notice trigger EXISTS again after the rebuild, and after a rolled-back
  one — drop-and-recreate must not leave the database without it.
- A projected landing naming a session id this database does not have lands
  with `session_id` NULL rather than failing the insert.

# Largely subsumed by write-once `sessions.task_id` (E-1969 and the tightening)

Re-analysed 2026-08-16 after the requester pointed out that a bind which can
never be reassigned is the FEATURE, not the failure. They are right, and the
original framing of this task was wrong.

## Why write-once fixes the reported symptom

`session resume E-1953` resumes an EXISTING Claude session by UUID, so the
`sessions` row already exists with `task_id = 1953`. `trySpawnBind` firing at
SessionStart is therefore a REASSIGNMENT of an already-bound session, not a
first bind. Under write-once semantics that write is refused and E-1953 stands.
No marker change needed for this case.

That is the entirety of the reported incident (twice), so the tightening
resolves it.

## The residual case, which write-once makes WORSE rather than better

A genuinely NEW Claude session started in a window left over from a previous
spawn. There the stale marker is the FIRST write, so write-once cements the
wrong task permanently — and the manual `task bind` recovery is gone by design.

Scope of that risk, measured rather than assumed:

- `task spawn` always creates a FRESH tmux window (`new-window`) and sets
  `@endless_spawned_by`, `@endless_task_id`, `@endless_project_id` on it
  (spawnlaunchcmd/tmux_driver.go, windowOptionCommands).
- Nothing anywhere clears any of the three.
- So the markers are per-window and die with the window. Exposure is confined
  to a spawned window that OUTLIVES its session and is then reused for
  something else.

That is narrow, but it is not theoretical: it is exactly the shape of the
incident that produced this task, differing only in whether the session was
resumed or fresh.

## Recommended shape, if it is still worth doing

CORRECTION (2026-08-16): an earlier draft of this analysis said not to clear the
window variables because it would break the E-1700 read race. That was wrong.
E-1700's race is `@endless_task_id` reading EMPTY, in which case `trySpawnBind`
returns false and binds nothing — so the variables must survive that path for
the retry, and they do. Clearing only after a bind SUCCEEDS preserves the retry
entirely.

So the fix is the obvious one: **`trySpawnBind` clears `@endless_spawned_by`
and `@endless_task_id` once it has successfully bound.** One spawn, one bind.
A later session starting in the same window finds nothing and falls through to
the cwd-based bind, which is correct for it.

Recording an expected session identity at spawn time is NOT viable as an
alternative: `task spawn` launches `claude` and the Claude session UUID does not
exist until the process starts, so spawn has nothing to record.

## Sequencing

Blocked on the write-once change rather than duplicating it. If that lands
first, re-scope this to the residual case only; the title should change with it,
since "clear the markers" is no longer the recommended fix.

## Requester position (2026-08-16): enforce the invariant, don't tolerate the breach

`tmux window == Claude session == Endless task` is to be treated as an
invariant. A new Claude session starting in a window left over from a previous
spawn should be made to FAIL, not quietly bound to something. Allowing the
invariant to break cascades: the tmux status line already resolves by WINDOW,
not pane, so a window associated with two sessions is ambiguous to it
independently of any binding bug.

Two mechanical facts that constrain how this can be built:

1. **SessionStart cannot hard-refuse a session.** The hook's only lever there is
   `additionalContext` — `handleWorktreeAdoption` already returns a "refusal"
   that is nothing more than injected text. Making a session genuinely unusable
   requires blocking at PreToolUse, which is the shape `enforceWorktreeGate` and
   `enforceClaimedCwd` already use. So "fail to run" = inform at SessionStart +
   block tool calls at PreToolUse.

2. **E-1669 faced this choice and went the other way**, deliberately: "A
   warning, NOT a refuse: refusing in the hook path blocks every tool call."
   That was the right call for its risk (a session dogfooding the wrong binary).
   The risk here is different in kind — under write-once `task_id` a mis-bind is
   permanent and has no recovery — which is what justifies the stronger
   response rather than copying E-1669's.

**Ship an escape hatch with the gate, or the gate becomes the bug.** Nothing in
the codebase clears `@endless_spawned_by` / `@endless_task_id` /
`@endless_project_id` today. If a window can be refused on the strength of those
markers, there must be a supported way to reset them — otherwise the first false
positive strands a tmux window permanently and the only workaround a user will
find is killing the window or disabling the gate.

Relationship to the identity-scoping fix above: they do different jobs and both
are worth having. Identity-scoped markers stop the WRONG BIND (a fresh session
falls through to the cwd bind, which is correct). The refusal enforces the
INVARIANT, which matters beyond binding because window-keyed resolution exists
elsewhere. Scoping is the narrower, safer change; refusal is the architectural
one and carries the false-positive risk.

---

# Addendum — E-1969 landed; re-scoped to the residual case (2026-08-25)

VOCABULARY. The sections above call them "markers". They are tmux WINDOW
OPTIONS — key/value pairs tmux stores per window, readable with
`tmux show-options -w` and by `tmux display-message -p -t <pane> '#{@name}'`.
`task spawn` sets three of them on the window it creates; a fourth is written by
the hook. A spawned window looks like this:

    @endless_project_id     1
    @endless_session_uuid   f4374aaf-b432-495a-b377-351068e8dfb8
    @endless_spawned_by     1137
    @endless_task_id        1969

Below this line the term "window option" is used instead of "marker".

Written from ES's E-1969 session at Mike's request. Evidence and scope only; the
choice between the two shapes below is still Mike's to
settle.

## The reported symptom is now fixed, in the database

`sessions.task_id` is write-once as of E-1969, enforced by the
`sessions_task_id_write_once` trigger. The resume case plays out like this now,
verified against the shipped code:

1. `trySpawnBind` reads the stale `@endless_task_id` and calls
   `BindSessionToTask`.
2. The row already holds a task, so the write is a reassignment and the trigger
   aborts it. `BindSessionToTask` returns an error naming "write-once".
3. `trySpawnBind` logs and returns FALSE, so `maybeCwdBind` runs
   `autoBindFromCwd`, which E-1856 already guards against re-pointing.
4. The correct binding stands.

No marker change is needed for that case. `session resume E-1953` can no longer
be stolen by a leftover marker.

## What is left, and why write-once makes it worse

A genuinely NEW session in a window a previous spawn left behind. `task_id` is
NULL, so the stale marker is the FIRST write and the trigger PERMITS it. The
wrong task is then permanent: E-1968 made `task bind` first-set-only and E-1969
enforces it in the database, so the manual recovery this task's original
incident used is gone by design.

Before E-1969 this was a recoverable annoyance. After it, it is unrecoverable.
That inversion is the whole remaining case, and it is the reason to keep this
task open rather than close it as subsumed.

## Defect in the recommended shape above — do not build it as written

The "Recommended shape" section says `trySpawnBind` should clear
`@endless_spawned_by` AND `@endless_task_id` once it has bound. Clearing
`@endless_spawned_by` is wrong: it is not only a bind trigger.
`monitor.ResolveSessionStatusParentSession` reads that same window option to
render the `from` provenance row in `session status`
(`internal/monitor/session_status.go`, and the note at
`internal/sessionstatuscmd/session_status.go` about keeping that row testable
headless). Clearing it at the first SessionStart erases the window's parent-
session link for the rest of its life.

CORRECTION, same day: the two paragraphs that stood here proposed unsetting
`@endless_task_id` instead, and a new `@endless_bound_session` option as a
variant. Both were wrong. See "Unsetting any marker is out" and "The window
already carries the facts" below, which replace them. Recorded rather than
deleted because the reasoning that produced them is the thing to avoid
repeating.

E-1700's retry is unaffected by any of this and is worth keeping straight: that
race is `@endless_task_id` reading EMPTY, in which case `trySpawnBind` returns
false and binds nothing, so the next SessionStart retries.

## Unsetting a window option is out

Not "clear `@endless_spawned_by` but `@endless_task_id` is fine" — unsetting is
wrong for either one, for two independent reasons.

### It destroys a value that other readers depend on

`@endless_task_id` is not only `trySpawnBind`'s trigger.

`endless session status` has to decide which task the view is ABOUT. It tries
three sources in order, and stops at the first that answers: (1) the task held
by a live session in this window; (2) the window's own `@endless_task_id`;
(3) the most-recent live session. Source (2) is the one at issue — it is what
answers when no live session is found, which is exactly the state a window is in
after its spawned session ends. Unset it and `session status` in that window
loses its subject.

E-1302 (`endless task id` / `endless tmux task`, spawned 2026-08-25) proposes
reading the same window option as a user-facing lookup, so it would lose its
answer too.

### It conflates two states that must stay distinct

Absent has to mean one thing, and unsetting would give it two:

- **(a) This window WAS created by `task spawn`, and its one bind already
  happened.** The state unsetting is trying to record.
- **(b) This window was never created by `task spawn` at all.** The ordinary
  case: a tmux window opened by hand, `claude` started in it. `task spawn` never
  touched it, so it has no `@endless_*` options and never did.

Both read as "no `@endless_task_id`". Nothing downstream can tell them apart.

Whether that matters depends on what is being built, which is why it is decisive
here. For "just do not bind twice" it does not — (a) and (b) both want the same
outcome, fall through to the cwd bind. For a gate that REFUSES, it is fatal:
(a) is the breach to refuse and (b) is a completely ordinary window that must
never be refused. Unsetting destroys precisely the distinction the gate is made
of.

Encoding a fact by destroying the evidence for it is also the class of write
E-1898 removed from `sessions`, and for the same reason: the erased value is
what you need when the thing goes wrong.

## The window already carries the facts — the question is which id is durable

A spawned window carries four options today:

    @endless_project_id    @endless_spawned_by
    @endless_task_id       @endless_session_uuid

`@endless_session_uuid` is E-1585's, written by `setTmuxSessionUUID` in
`internal/hookcmd/claude.go`, so no new option needs inventing to record "which
session is in this window".

Two facts about it that constrain how it can be used, and one conclusion.

**Today it is overwritten on EVERY event**, before the SessionStart handling
that would read it — deliberately, so it self-heals after a tmux server restart.
As written it therefore records the most recent session in the window, not the
one the window was spawned for.

**Freezing it would be the wrong fix.** The value is a harness-issued
conversation id, and E-2063 measured that a clear rotates it (resume and
compaction do not). Making a rotating handle sticky does not turn it into an
identity; it turns it into a stale handle, and it breaks what E-1585 built the
option FOR — a sibling shell pane reading it to discover the Claude session
beside it would resolve a conversation that no longer exists. E-2063 names this
error class directly, in rejecting `CLAUDE_PID` as an anchor: "the general error
was reaching for a RUNTIME HANDLE as a DURABLE IDENTITY."

**So publish the id Endless owns instead.** Once E-2063 exists that is
`sessions.id`, which never rotates — at which point overwrite-vs-write-once
stops being a question at all, because writing the same value every event is
idempotent. The option stays self-healing AND stable across a clear, with no
invariant to enforce. This is the same move E-1969 made one table over:
`sessions.task_id` is write-once because Endless mints it; `sessions.session_id`
is not that kind of id, which is why E-2063 moves it out rather than freezing
it.

## E-1128 wants the opposite of a clear

E-1128 ("Record spawn lineage on `endless task spawn`", unplanned) treats
`@endless_spawned_by` as durable lineage. Partly stale — the marker exists today
and is already read for the provenance row — but whichever branch is chosen here
must not erase it, or E-1128's premise goes with it.

## Why Branch B is not merely a bigger Branch A

`monitor.GetTaskForPane` resolves pane-specific first, then falls back to WINDOW
scope: any pane in the same window with a non-NULL `task_id`, most recent
`last_activity` winning. So a window that has hosted two sessions on two tasks
gives the status line an answer decided by a timestamp race, independently of
whether either binding was correct. Marker scoping does not touch that; the
invariant gate is what would. Branch A fixes an instance, Branch B fixes a
class. That is the real difference between them, and it is not visible from the
binding bug alone.

## Sequencing note

E-1972 (underway) may invert which binary runs the Claude hooks. Whatever lands
here lives in `internal/hookcmd/claude.go` on the SessionStart path, so it will
sit underneath that decision. Not a conflict — overlap to coordinate, in that
order.

---

# The invariant, as the requester states it (2026-08-25)

Superseding the 2026-08-16 "Requester position" section above, which said
`tmux window == Claude session == Endless task`. That form cannot hold, because
a clear mints a new harness session id. The form that does:

    tmux window == Endless task == one or more Claude sessions

with two explicit non-accommodations:

- NOT multiple CONCURRENT sessions for the same task.
- NOT multiple ACTIVE tmux windows for the same task.

Sessions in SERIES are accommodated; sessions in PARALLEL are not. That is the
whole of it, and it is what makes the gate expressible: the thing being counted
is the Endless session, not the harness conversation.

# Decided 2026-08-25: two window options, two jobs

- **`@endless_session_uuid` keeps its current behaviour** — overwritten on every
  event, meaning "the CURRENT Claude session in this window". That is correct for
  what E-1585 built it for and must not be frozen.
- **Add `@endless_session_id`, carrying `sessions.id`** — the durable identity
  Endless mints and owns. It is the one a gate may compare against.

Two options because they answer two different questions: which conversation is
live in this window right now, and which Endless session this window belongs to.
Neither can do the other's job.

# The one question left

Everything else above is settled. What is not:

**When the window says task T and the starting session's cwd says task M, which
source wins — and is the disagreement resolved silently or refused?**

That is the whole of it, and every earlier framing of this task collapses into
it. The three answers are the three behaviours that have been discussed:

- **Window wins.** Today's behaviour, and the bug: `trySpawnBind` binds to T,
  returns true, and suppresses the cwd bind that would have said M. Under
  write-once that is now permanent.
- **cwd wins.** `trySpawnBind` defers when the two disagree; `autoBindFromCwd`
  binds M. Silent, small, and correct for the ordinary case. Reaches the same
  end state the old "clear the markers" shape aimed at, with nothing unset.
- **Refuse.** The disagreement is the invariant breach; the session is informed
  at SessionStart and blocked at PreToolUse. Enforces the invariant rather than
  papering over it, and costs a false-positive budget plus an escape hatch.

Why it is one question and not two: "what does it compare" is already answered —
`@endless_task_id` against `resolveCwdTaskID`, which is the signal
`autoBindFromCwd` already trusts, and which needs no window option to be
mutated. Only the policy on mismatch is open.

Two sub-cases the chosen answer has to cover, neither of which changes the shape
of the question:

- **cwd is not in any worktree** (the main checkout, or anywhere else). The cwd
  source has no answer, so there is no disagreement to detect — only the window's
  claim. Refusing here would refuse a great many ordinary windows.
- **After E-2063, the session may be a new INSTANCE of the window's own Endless
  session** (a clear). That is not a disagreement at all and must never be
  refused; `payload.Source` distinguishes it today (`clear` vs `startup`), and
  E-2063 may make it structural.

Independent of the answer: nothing clears any of the four window options, so a
window refused on their strength has no supported reset. If the answer is
"refuse", the reset ships with it or the first false positive strands the window.

# Corrections to the addendum above, for the record

- The addendum's "Defect in the recommended shape" originally concluded that
  `@endless_task_id` could be consumed by unsetting. Replaced in place; see
  "Unsetting any marker is out".
- An earlier draft of this analysis cited E-1640 as evidence that a succession
  of session rows per window is normal and supported. That inverts what E-1640
  says: it is titled "Fix duplicate session rows minted per Claude launch when
  TMUX_PANE is empty" and its remedy ENDS the extra rows. It treated the
  succession as a defect to suppress, which is the opposite of blessing it.
  E-2063 is where that model actually changes.
- The addendum used the word "marker" throughout without ever defining it. It
  means an `@endless_*` tmux window option; see the VOCABULARY note at the head
  of the addendum. New text says "window option".

# Plan

Three landable increments. Each leaves the tree green and shippable; do not
start the next until the previous has landed.

## Increment 1 — the tables, written but not yet authoritative

New schema change file `internal/schema/changes/e-2063-session-instances.sql`,
mirrored into `internal/schema/schema.sql`.

```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS session_instances (
    id            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    session_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES sessions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    harness       TEXT    NOT NULL,
    first_seen_at TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT (strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S','now')),
    last_event_at TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT (strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S','now')),
    ended_at      TEXT,
    recap         TEXT,
    recap_through TEXT,
    UNIQUE (id, harness)
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS claude_cli_sessions (
    instance_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    harness     TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (harness = 'claude_cli'),
    uuid        TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    FOREIGN KEY (instance_id, harness)
        REFERENCES session_instances (id, harness)
);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS session_instances_by_session
    ON session_instances (session_id, first_seen_at);
```

NO `UNIQUE (session_id) WHERE ended_at IS NULL`. `ended_at` is display-only —
see the analysis; adding that index re-opens a settled decision.

Backfill in the same change file: one instance per existing `sessions` row,
`first_seen_at` from `sessions.started_at`, `last_event_at` from
`sessions.last_activity`, `harness` from `sessions.platform`, `ended_at` set
when `state='ended'`, and a `claude_cli_sessions` row carrying
`sessions.session_id` where that is non-empty and `platform='claude'`.

Nothing reads the new tables yet. Land here.

## Increment 2 — resolution moves to the instance

`sessions.session_id` stays in place and keeps being written, so this increment
is reversible; it stops being the resolution key, not the stored value.

- `monitor.GetActiveSession(uuid)` resolves uuid -> `claude_cli_sessions` ->
  `session_instances` -> `sessions`, returning the Endless session.
- `monitor.TouchSession` upserts the INSTANCE (bumping `last_event_at`, clearing
  a stale `ended_at`), and upserts the `sessions` row only when no instance
  matches the uuid.
- SessionStart: when the window/task already has a session and the uuid is new,
  append an instance rather than inserting a `sessions` row. `payload.Source`
  (`startup`/`resume`/`clear`/`compact`) is currently read nowhere; read it here
  and treat anything other than `startup` as continuation.
- Close the prior instance (`ended_at`) when a clear appends a new one.
- `session_messages.session_id` FKs `sessions(session_id)` — the uuid, not the
  id. Re-point it at `session_instances.id` so a clear gives later transcript
  rows a new parent and no prior row is rewritten.
- Move `platform` off `sessions`; `session_instances.harness` is the single
  discriminator.

Leave alone in this increment: `session_gates`, `session_tasks`,
`session_navigations`, `decisions.origin_session_id`, `task_landings`,
`project_next_events`, `report_labels`. All key on `sessions.id`, which does not
change, so none of them move.

## Increment 3 — the collapse, and the CLI

- Collapse the multiple `sessions` rows per task that exist today (E-1307 has 7;
  1362 and 1322 have 6). Keep the EARLIEST row by `started_at` as the surviving
  session; convert the rest to instances of it; re-point the seven FK-holding
  tables above at the survivor. Verify against the pre-migration row counts.
- `resume` refuses when a session has 2+ instances with `ended_at IS NULL`:
  print them ordered by `first_seen_at` ASC with ordinal, `first_seen_at`,
  `last_event_at`, message count and recap, and exit non-zero. Never close one
  automatically. `--instance <ordinal|uuid>` selects.
- `resume` and `goto --resume` share ONE resolver.
- Delete `spawn --new-session`. Replace with `--fresh-context` if the
  "do not inherit prior context into the handoff" behaviour is still wanted.
- Split `spawn --reopen` into `reopen` (task-status verb) and `resume` (session
  verb; restores the worktree, navigates when a live owner exists).

# Verification

`tests/tasks/e-2063-verify.sh`, fail-fast on units then end-to-end through the
real hook against the sandbox DB (drive it with an explicit `--config-dir`, per
`tests/tasks/e-1953-verify.sh` — without that flag the hook's PinMainDB sends
writes to the REAL ledger).

1. A clear appends: feed SessionStart with a NEW uuid and `source=clear` for a
   window whose session exists; assert exactly one `sessions` row for the task
   before and after, and one more `session_instances` row after.
2. Resume does not append: same, `source=resume` with the existing uuid; assert
   the instance count is unchanged.
3. The prior instance is closed on a clear; the surviving one has
   `ended_at IS NULL`.
4. A stale `ended_at` blocks nothing: leave two instances open, insert a third,
   assert it succeeds. This is the regression guard on the rejected index.
5. `resume` with 2+ open instances exits non-zero, lists them ordered by
   `first_seen_at` ASC, and closes nothing — assert `ended_at` values are
   identical before and after.
6. `--instance` selects by both ordinal and uuid.
7. A `claude_cli_sessions` row cannot attach to a non-`claude_cli` instance —
   assert the composite FK rejects it.
8. Migration: pre/post counts for the seven FK-holding tables, and every task
   with multiple `sessions` rows ends with exactly one.
9. `sessions.platform` is gone and nothing references it.

Not verifiable by test: whether one open instance per session is actually
maintained in the field. Nothing enforces it at the storage layer by design —
that is E-1983's invariant gate plus write-once `task_id`.

fields.title: Refuse `rebuild-db --confirm` deliberately instead of by accident
fields.description: `rebuild-db --confirm` aborts on any project with a session bound to a task, and that abort is load-bearing: with it removed, the same DELETE destroys task_landings, session_gates and — via a second cascade hop — report_judgments and report_labels, none of which the copy-back restores. It also nulls sessions.task_id, which ED-1560 forbids. Replace the accidental fuse with an explicit up-front refusal that counts what would be lost and names E-799 as the owner of the actual repair. Does NOT fix the rebuild.
fields.text:
# Plan: make `rebuild-db --confirm` refuse deliberately

`rebuild-db --confirm` cannot run today and MUST NOT be made to run. It aborts
on any project with a session bound to a task, and that abort is the only thing
standing between the command and a large amount of unrecoverable data. This task
replaces the accident with an intention. It does NOT repair the rebuild — that
belongs to **E-799**, the event-sourcing epic, which is where "SQLite as a
rebuildable projection" is actually owned.

## What the command does today, measured

`runRebuildDB` (`internal/eventcmd/event.go`) replays the ledger into a scratch
database, then copies back exactly three tables: `tasks`, `decisions`,
`decision_relations`. The copy is spelled as `DELETE FROM <table>` followed by
`INSERT ... SELECT * FROM proj.<table>`.

The full transitive closure of that `DELETE FROM tasks`, derived from
`pragma_foreign_key_list` over a fresh schema, not by reading:

| Reached                     | Action   | Restored? |
|-----------------------------|----------|-----------|
| `task_landings`             | CASCADE  | **no — destroyed** |
| `session_gates` (`epic_id`) | CASCADE  | **no — destroyed** |
| → `report_judgments`        | CASCADE  | **no — destroyed (second hop)** |
| → `report_labels`           | CASCADE  | **no — destroyed (second hop)** |
| `sessions.task_id`          | SET NULL | no |
| `sessions.epic_id`          | SET NULL | no |
| `session_statuses.task_id`  | SET NULL | no |
| `decisions.origin_task_id`  | SET NULL | yes |
| `tasks.parent_id`           | SET NULL | yes |

Two of those are SECOND-HOP: `session_gates` cascades onward. Anything that
walks only the direct children of `tasks` will miss them.

`task_deps` is a fourth gap of a different kind: the projector builds it, the
copy-back skips it, and no FK reaches it — so a rebuild silently leaves every
blocking relation at whatever the live database happened to hold.

And per **E-1041**, the projection's INPUT is already known-bad: replay logs FK
and UNIQUE failures, and committed test fixtures reuse real task ids 1–150 in
~36 of 47 ledger segments. So the output cannot be trusted even where the
copy-back is correct.

## The one thing this task builds

Refuse in `runRebuildDB`, BEFORE the projection is built and before any
transaction opens, whenever `--confirm` is passed. Print what the command would
destroy — counted from the live database, not described in the abstract:

    rebuild-db --confirm is disabled: it would destroy data the ledger cannot
    restore.

      N task_landings rows      (landing history)
      N session_gates rows      (and N report_judgments, N report_labels)
      N sessions bindings       (violates ED-1560)
      task_deps                 not rebuilt at all — left stale

    The projection is also unreliable while E-1041 is open.
    Repairing this is E-799. Do not remove the write-once trigger or the
    `ON DELETE SET NULL` on sessions.task_id to make this command run — see
    "Sequencing" in E-2062.

The dry run (no `--confirm`) keeps working exactly as it does now: it is
read-only, it builds the projection, it prints counts. That is the useful half
of the command and this task does not touch it.

## Sequencing — the trap this task exists to disarm

`sessions.task_id ON DELETE SET NULL` is a STANDING VIOLATION of ED-1560. The
invariant says the binding is set once and never cleared; the FK says it is
cleared whenever the task row goes. It has never fired only because tasks are
almost never deleted and because the write-once trigger aborts it when they are.
`session_tasks` already documents the correct shape — no FK at all, so "rows
must outlive their referenced session/task."

So the FK action is wrong and should eventually go. **But removing it also
removes the abort**, and the abort is what currently prevents the four CASCADE
rows above from being destroyed in silence. Fixing the schema first converts a
loud refusal into quiet data loss.

The order is therefore fixed:

1. This task's explicit guard.
2. E-799 makes the rebuild whole (copy back what the projector builds; suppress
   the notice triggers; decide what `task_deps` and the session tables mean).
3. Only then drop `sessions.task_id`'s FK action, and delete this guard.

Write step 3 down here because step 3 looks obviously correct in isolation.

## Traps for whoever does the repair under E-799

Recorded now, while they are measured, so the repair does not rediscover them:

- **An upsert fires `tasks_notify_sessions`.** It is `AFTER UPDATE ON tasks`, so
  today's delete-then-insert never triggers it, but replacing that pair with
  `ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE` would notify every live session about every task
  whose projected value differs. The notice triggers must be suppressed for the
  duration of any copy-back, the way
  `internal/schema/changes/e-1969-rename-sessions-task-id.go` drops and
  re-creates a trigger inside its transaction.
- **Copying `task_landings` back fires `task_landings_notify_sessions`**
  (`AFTER INSERT`), announcing every historical landing to every live session.
  The E-2005 schema comment currently calls that replay "harmless" and says so
  ON THE GROUNDS that `event rebuild` copies back only three tables — correct
  today, wrong the moment the repair lands. Correct that comment in the same
  commit.
- **A projected `task_landings.session_id` may name a session this machine has
  never had.** The ledger is shareable; `sessions` is machine-local. NULL it on
  copy rather than failing the FK.
- **`PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF` is not the way out.** SQLite ignores it inside a
  transaction, so it would have to fence the whole replacement — and then a
  genuinely-lost task id is deleted with enforcement off, leaving dangling rows.
  It trades a loud abort for silent corruption, which is the same trade as
  dropping the trigger. (`monitor.DB()` sets `SetMaxOpenConns(1)`, so the usual
  pooled-connection objection does NOT apply here.)

## Not in scope

- `session_statuses` is a dead feature being removed under separate work. Count
  it in the refusal if it still exists when this is built; do not design around
  it and do not remove it here.
- `decisions` / `decision_relations` are self-consistent: the only dependent
  cascades and is replaced in the same transaction. Leave them alone.

## Verification

- `rebuild-db --confirm` refuses on a database with a bound session, naming the
  counts, and writes NOTHING — assert the row counts of `task_landings`,
  `session_gates`, `report_judgments`, `report_labels` and `sessions.task_id`
  are identical before and after.
- It refuses on a database with NO bound session too. The guard is about what
  the command would destroy, not about whether the trigger happens to catch it —
  a project with landings but no bindings is the case today's accidental fuse
  misses entirely.
- The dry run (no `--confirm`) still builds the projection and prints its counts,
  unchanged.
- The write-once trigger and every `REFERENCES tasks(id)` clause are still
  declared in `schema.sql`: assert it, so a later sweep cannot "fix" the abort by
  removing the fuse.
